title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
This is the closing page of a problem begun on the previous page. Among all space curves, find the one that makes ∫ w ds a maximum or minimum, where w is an arbitrary function of the distance v = OZ = √(x²+y²+z²) from a fixed point O. Euler had first solved this directly in three dimensions, 'per tantas ambages' (by such roundabout ways). In §43–44 he observes that the integrand involves only two quantities, the distance and the arc element. So the problem can be posed for a plane curve described about a centre C.

Polar coordinates are used: x = radius CZ and y = the angle DCZ. Then ds = √(dx² + x² dy²). With dy = p dx the functional becomes ∫ w(x) √(1 + p²x²) dx, so V = w √(1 + p²x²).

In Euler's isoperimetric notation, dV = M dx + N dy + P dp, and the Euler–Lagrange equation is N dx = dP. Here the angle y is a cyclic (ignorable) variable, so N = 0. Hence dP = 0, giving the first integral
  P = w p x² / √(1 + p²x²) = C.
This says that w · x · sin ψ is constant, where ψ is the angle between the curve and the radius.

In §45 Euler solves for p: p = C / (x √(w²x² − C²)). This gives the angle as a quadrature, y = ∫ C dx / (x √(w²x² − C²)). Euler notes that this agrees with his earlier laborious three-dimensional solution once x is renamed v and y is renamed φ. He closes with a methodological moral: very hard problems can often be made very easy by a slight transformation.
errors: Printed '∂y = ∫ c∂x/(x√(wwx²−cc))' mixes notation; it should read y = ∫ c∂x/(x√(wwx²−cc)), or ∂y = c∂x/(x√(...)).
On the previous page the integrand is misprinted as √(∂x² + yy∂y²); it should be √(∂x² + xx∂y²). The next line (∫ w∂x √(1+ppxx)) is correct.
The algebra p² x² (w²x² − C²) = C² checks out. The sign and branch issues and the case C = 0 (radial lines) are not discussed; this is minor.

ideas.what: Reducing a spatial variational problem with a radially symmetric weight to a planar polar problem: the extremal lies in a plane through the centre.
ideas.modern_name: Symmetry reduction / conservation of angular momentum implies planar motion
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Newton, for central forces); variationally, Euler and Lagrange
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (1744), Additamentum II (motion under central forces via ∫ v ds); E740 itself

ideas.what: A cyclic coordinate yields the first integral P = ∂V/∂p = const, i.e. w x sin ψ = const.
ideas.modern_name: Noether-type first integral for an ignorable coordinate; Bouguer's / Clairaut's relation (n r sin ψ = const)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Bouguer (refraction in a spherically stratified atmosphere), Clairaut (geodesics on surfaces of revolution), Euler (variational form)
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (1744), case where V lacks y

ideas.what: The trajectory obtained as a quadrature: y = ∫ C dx / (x √(w²x² − C²)).
ideas.modern_name: Central-force orbit equation / ray equation in a radially symmetric medium

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard reduction: a cyclic coordinate gives a first integral, recovering the known central-force and ray quadrature. Euler himself presents it as a didactic remark about choosing good variables. Nothing here is absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reproduces the printed '∂y = ∫ ...'; this is a typographical error in the original and should be y = ∫ ....
The image shows 'C' (capital) in P = ... = C and lowercase 'c' in §45. These are the same constant.
